The [blue whale](/wiki/Blue_whale "Blue whale") is the heaviest living animal.

The heaviest living animals are all [whales](/wiki/Whale "Whale"). There are considerable obstacles to overcome in obtaining accurate weights for them, however, as no scale can accommodate the whole body of a large whale. Whaling factories are usually enlisted to help accomplish the task, but it still remains difficult, and most weighings have been done by parts of flensed whales, leaving much room for error. Mathematical formulas have also been devised to estimate the average weight of various whale species based on body length, but this method is equally prone to inaccuracy.[[22]](#cite_note-22)

It was the largest building in Philadelphia at the time, and thousands of people attended it to hear Whitefield preach.[[31]](#cite_note-MontgomeryHistory-36): 26

In the fall of 1749, [Benjamin Franklin](/wiki/Benjamin_Franklin "Benjamin Franklin"), a [Founding Father](/wiki/Founding_Fathers_of_the_United_States "Founding Fathers of the United States") and [polymath](/wiki/Polymath "Polymath") in Philadelphia, circulated a pamphlet, "[Proposals Relating to the Education of Youth in Pensilvania](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Proposals_Relating_to_the_Education_of_Youth_in_Pensilvania_(UC)_-_Benjamin_Franklin_(1931_1749).djvu "commons:File:Proposals Relating to the Education of Youth in Pensilvania (UC) - Benjamin Franklin (1931 1749).djvu")," his vision for what he called a "Public Academy of Philadelphia".[[32]](#cite_note-37)

Penn identifies as the [fourth-oldest institution of higher education in the United States](/wiki/List_of_oldest_universities_in_continuous_operation "List of oldest universities in continuous operation"), though this representation is challenged by [Princeton](/wiki/Princeton_University "Princeton University") and [Columbia](/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University") since the College of Philadelphia was not chartered or commence classes until 1755 and the first board of trustees was not convened until 1749, arguably making it the sixth or fifth-oldest.[[b]](#cite_note-founding_note-9)

The annual G7 summit is attended by each member's head of government.[[78]](#cite_note-feldman1-78) The member country holding the G7 presidency is responsible for organizing and hosting the year's summit. The serial annual summits can be parsed chronologically in arguably distinct ways, including as the sequence of host countries for the summits has recurred over time and series.[[79]](#cite_note-79) Generally every country hosts the summit once every seven years.[[80]](#cite_note-80)

Besides a main meeting in June or July, a number of other meetings may take place throughout the year; in 2021 for example, seven tracks existed for finance (4–5 June 2021), environmental (20 and 21 May 2021), health (3–4 June 2021), trade (27–28 May 2021), interior (7–9 September 2021) digital and technology (28–29 April 2021), development (3–5 May 2021) and foreign ministers.[[81]](#cite_note-ministers-81)

Not to be confused with [Tetraedron](/wiki/Tetraedron "Tetraedron") or [Tetrahedron (journal)](/wiki/Tetrahedron_(journal) "Tetrahedron (journal)").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/Triangular_pyramid1.png/250px-Triangular_pyramid1.png)](/wiki/File:Triangular_pyramid1.png)

A tetrahedron.

In [geometry](/wiki/Geometry "Geometry"), a **tetrahedron** (pl.: **tetrahedra** or **tetrahedrons**), also known as a  **triangular pyramid**, is a [polyhedron](/wiki/Polyhedron "Polyhedron") composed of four triangular [faces](/wiki/Face_(geometry) "Face (geometry)"), six straight [edges](/wiki/Edge_(geometry) "Edge (geometry)"), and four [vertices](/wiki/Vertex_(geometry) "Vertex (geometry)"). The tetrahedron is the simplest of all the ordinary [convex polyhedra](/wiki/Convex_polytope "Convex polytope").[[1]](#cite_note-MW-1)

The tetrahedron is the [three-dimensional](/wiki/Three-dimensional "Three-dimensional") case of the more general concept of a [Euclidean](/wiki/Euclidean_geometry "Euclidean geometry") [simplex](/wiki/Simplex "Simplex"), and may thus also be called a **3-simplex**.

The tetrahedron is one kind of [pyramid](/wiki/Pyramid_(geometry) "Pyramid (geometry)"), which is a polyhedron with a flat [polygon](/wiki/Polygon "Polygon") base and triangular faces connecting the base to a common point. In the case of a tetrahedron, the base is a [triangle](/wiki/Triangle "Triangle") (any of the four faces can be considered the base), so a tetrahedron is also known as a "triangular pyramid".

Like all [convex polyhedra](/wiki/Convex_polyhedra "Convex polyhedra"), a tetrahedron can be folded from a single sheet of paper. It has two such [nets](/wiki/Net_(polyhedron) "Net (polyhedron)").[[2]](#cite_note-2)

For any tetrahedron there exists a sphere (called the [circumsphere](/wiki/Circumsphere "Circumsphere")) on which all four vertices lie, and another sphere (the [insphere](/wiki/Insphere "Insphere")) [tangent](/wiki/Tangent "Tangent") to the tetrahedron's faces.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

It has a population estimated at over 13 million residents within the city limits,[[5]](#cite_note-2021Census-5) over 19.1 million residents in the urban area,[[6]](#cite_note-Urban-6) and over 21.5 million residents in [its metropolitan area](/wiki/Moscow_metropolitan_area "Moscow metropolitan area").[[14]](#cite_note-Megapolis-15) The city covers an area of 2,511 square kilometers (970 mi2), while the urban area covers 5,891 square kilometers (2,275 mi2),[[6]](#cite_note-Urban-6) and the metropolitan area covers over 26,000 square kilometers (10,000 mi2).[[14]](#cite_note-Megapolis-15) Moscow is among the world's [largest cities](/wiki/List_of_largest_cities "List of largest cities"), being the [most populous city](/wiki/List_of_European_cities_by_population_within_city_limits "List of European cities by population within city limits") entirely in Europe,[[b]](#cite_note-16) the largest [urban](/wiki/List_of_urban_areas_in_Europe "List of urban areas in Europe") and [metropolitan area](/wiki/List_of_metropolitan_areas_in_Europe "List of metropolitan areas in Europe") in Europe,[[6]](#cite_note-Urban-6)[[14]](#cite_note-Megapolis-15) and the largest city by land area on the European continent.[[15]](#cite_note-Planète_Énergies-17)

First documented in 1147, Moscow became the capital of the [Grand Principality of Moscow](/wiki/Grand_Principality_of_Moscow "Grand Principality of Moscow"), which led the unification of the Russian lands in the 15th century and became the center of a unified state.[[16]](#cite_note-18) Following the proclamation of the [Tsardom of Russia](/wiki/Tsardom_of_Russia "Tsardom of Russia") in 1547, Moscow remained the political and economic center for most of its history.
